items.title: Split the ADR record into per-decision files and generate the index
items.outcome: Every architecture decision lives in its own fixed-name file, with generated index and pending slots in adr/README.md. Nine ordinary, disjoint decision additions can integrate without shared-line conflicts; supersessions declare and serialize their overlapping derived predecessor effects.
items.context: The presplit adr/README.md holds fourteen accepted records and nine pending reservations. Per-decision sources and preallocated generated slots avoid shared-line edits for ordinary additions while retaining every accepted decision. Supersession is a distinct overlapping case: the generator derives predecessor status without rewriting decided source, and competing successors require semantic resolution.
scope: Per-ADR file layout under adr/, one accepted decision per file, with the numbered file name as the durable identifier
Migration of the fourteen accepted records into that layout with no content change
Header convention carrying number, title, recorded status/date, supersedes and superseded-by; mandatory owning ticket claim on new records, with no invented owner data on the fourteen legacy records
Generator that produces the index table and the pending execution-gate table in adr/README.md from the files
Reservation file as fixed owner allocation for ADR-015 to ADR-023, with current decision state derived from the ADR file rather than edited in the shared reservation data
Check that fails when a file's declared number, its file name or its index row disagree, and when a number is used twice

Single-ownership rule recorded in the parallel protocol: authors edit only owned ADR source and the generator writes authorized affected slots, including declared derived predecessor effects for supersession
Pinned raw presplit README reference retained in the candidate tree so complete legacy bodies and original allocations are validated independently of candidate HEAD in shallow CI
acceptance_criteria: Every accepted record from ADR-001 to ADR-014 exists as its own file; decision text is byte-identical apart from the added header and the owner-approved normalization of terminal LF separator bytes to one final LF. The full pinned pre-split reference and historical body hash/length inventory remain byte-exact; no interior whitespace or content normalization is permitted
adr/README.md carries generated regions for the accepted index and the pending gate table, delimited by markers, and running the generator on unchanged inputs rewrites nothing
A new record file appears in the index after running the generator, with no manual edit to adr/README.md

ADR-015 to ADR-023 are reserved to named tickets in a checked-in reservation file; a record claiming a reserved number from a different ticket fails the check, and the reservation state is derived from the ADR file rather than hand-edited
The check fails when two files declare the same number, when a file name and its declared number disagree, and when a generated region has been hand-edited
The protocol and ticket boundary agree: authors edit only owned ADR source, the generator alone updates authorized affected slots in decision worktrees, and no generated bytes are edited manually

Nine ordinary ADR-015 to ADR-023 additions preserve real owners, all canonical legacy split-file bytes and the exact original reference across committed serial squash sequences in forward, reverse and alternating orders and both adjacent-pair orders, with strict validation, exact rendering and cumulative record retention after every merge

Supersession derives reverse relationships and effective predecessor status without mutating predecessor source; self, dangling, cyclic and competing successor links fail, and overlapping generated effects are declared and serialized separately from the ordinary disjoint case
Committed candidate body/manifest drift, missing legacy records, missing fixed reservations, owner reassignment, unsupported schemas and metadata/body inconsistency fail even with a depth-1 checkout
contracts_schema: ADR header schema published in adr/LAYOUT.md: number, title, status, date, supersedes, superseded-by and mandatory ticket for nonlegacy records
Version-1 reservation data maps each reserved number to its owning ticket; explicit future allocations may extend but never drop or reassign the original nine
security_privacy: The generator reads and writes only files in the docs repository and consumes no credential
No decision content is rewritten by the generator; it produces index rows only
observability: The generated index shows allocated and claimed numbers and tickets; unallocated new numbers fail validation
A failed generation names the offending file and the rule it broke rather than printing a diff
tests: Idempotency test proving a second generator run produces no change
Duplicate-number and name-mismatch failure tests
Hand-edited generated region failure test
Real-allocation nine-branch fixtures with committed serial squash and both adjacent-pair orders; strict validation, exact render, owners and cumulative records checked after every step
Depth-1 local file-transport clone validates the pinned reference without parent history and rejects a committed invalid allocation
Separate missing/wrong/correct-owner, schema, recorded-status/date and supersession cases, including same-predecessor textual and semantic conflicts
rollout_rollback: The split lands as one pull request before any decision ticket starts, so no gate ticket ever sees the single-file layout
Before dependent decisions exist, rollback is a separately reviewed protected revert of the split pull request; validate the restored layout before resuming work

After dependent decisions exist, stop affected workstreams and review a preservation migration instead of a destructive revert; retain accepted source bodies and headers, original allocations, raw reference and historical body-hash manifest

For missing or truncated derived README output, the layout owner follows adr/LAYOUT.md: retain and validate all inputs before unscoped regeneration, verify unchanged sources afterward, and stop on missing or inconsistent inputs. Recover a partial split in isolation; never overwrite retained downstream work by restoring the raw monolith and rerunning split
non_goals: Deciding anything: this ticket moves and generates, it does not author or amend a record
Renumbering the accepted records ADR-001 to ADR-014
A documentation site, search or rendering pipeline
items.parallel_boundary: Primary repo docs. T-ADR-INDEX-10 owns the layout, allocation map and generator. Gate authors edit only their owned ADR source and use ticket-scoped generation for authorized affected slots, never manual generated bytes. Ordinary decisions update only their preallocated slots. Supersession additionally regenerates derived predecessor index/state slots without changing predecessor source; declare and serialize overlapping effects. Two successors of the same predecessor are not conflict-free. Allocation extensions are explicit and cannot drop or reassign the original nine owners.

items.title: ADR: money wire format, time and idempotency conventions
items.outcome: One record fixes how money, time and request identity cross every boundary, so no generated client can silently corrupt an amount and no retry can double-post.
items.context: The OpenAPI document currently types amounts as 64-bit integers, which generated TypeScript clients cannot represent safely. Time zones and idempotency keys are equally undecided, and both determine whether retries and scheduled jobs are correct.
scope: Integer minor units internally with canonical decimal strings at every JSON boundary
Generated domain wrapper types per language rather than raw primitives
Currency code carried with every amount and never inferred
Instants stored and transmitted in UTC with an explicit user time zone for calendar reasoning
Idempotency key semantics, scope, lifetime and conflict behaviour for all financial writes
Offline idempotency lifecycle: generate and persist before the first send, reuse unchanged for every retry, and define the loss and reinstall case
Cross-language representation caveats, including the bigint boundary limitation in TypeScript and the wrapper that hides it
Published as the reserved record ADR-015 in its own file under adr/, claimed from the T-ADR-INDEX-10 reservation file
Python representation for the ai-service: a Decimal-backed money wrapper with its currency, and the serialisation seam where it is constructed and destructed
acceptance_criteria: The record states the exact JSON representation for an amount and rejects raw floating point and raw 64-bit integers with a stated reason
Round-trip conversion between each language wrapper and the wire format is specified, including the maximum representable amount
The record states which endpoints require an idempotency key, how long a key is honoured and what a conflicting reuse returns
The record requires a client-generated key to be persisted before the first send and reused for every retry, and requires same-key-different-payload reuse to return one stable conflict response
The record states what happens after reinstall or local-queue loss, when the client no longer holds the original key, and which structured duplicate-detection path prevents a silent double post
The record states the storage and transport representation for instants and the rule for month and pay-period boundaries
A migration note explains what changes in the existing specification and which generated clients must be regenerated

The record states explicitly that a TypeScript bigint cannot cross a JSON boundary or a React Server Component boundary, so bigint is an internal representation only and the canonical decimal string with its currency remains the single wire and domain wrapper form
The record names the serialisation seam in each language where the wrapper is constructed and destructed, so no raw primitive escapes into application code
The record is merged as ADR-015 in its own file, and the generated index and pending table in adr/README.md are refreshed by the T-ADR-INDEX-10 generator rather than hand-edited
The record specifies the Python representation as a Decimal-backed wrapper carrying its currency, forbids float and bare int for money, and states the decimal context and rounding mode that apply
The record names the Python serialisation seam - where the canonical decimal string is parsed into the wrapper and rendered back - so no raw primitive escapes into ai-service application code
Round-trip conversion is specified for all three generated languages, Kotlin, TypeScript and Python, not two

items.title: ADR: category model as an append-only reporting dimension
items.outcome: Categories are settled as a reporting dimension distinct from ledger accounts, with defined split, as-of, merge and cycle semantics, so reporting can evolve without rewriting financial history.
items.context: Categories are currently modelled ambiguously as both ledger accounts and mergeable dimension records. The two readings produce different answers for historical reports and different migration costs, and every reporting, budgeting and AI ticket depends on which one is true.
scope: Categories as an append-only dimension; system ledger accounts remain stable and separate
Split allocations of a single transaction across several categories
As-of semantics so a historical report reflects the categorisation in force at the time or the current one, stated explicitly
Merge by redirect rather than destructive rewrite, with cycle prevention
Rules for user-defined versus system categories and for uncategorised records
Instalment categorisation: principal treated as a liability movement and interest as an expense
Published as the reserved record ADR-016 in its own file under adr/, claimed from the T-ADR-INDEX-10 reservation file
acceptance_criteria: The record states whether a category is ever a ledger account and rejects the alternative with a reason
Split allocations are specified to sum exactly to the transaction amount with a stated remainder rule
The record specifies whether reports are as-of-then or as-of-now and how a user switches view if both are offered
Merge redirect is specified as non-destructive, with the maximum redirect depth and the cycle prevention rule
The record states the effect on existing ingestion, budgeting, reporting and AI categorisation tickets
The record specifies split allocations across several categories including the rounding remainder rule, and requires the allocation to sum exactly to the transaction amount
The record specifies as-of-then and current-view reporting semantics precisely, states which is the default and states how a user switches between them
The record specifies merge as a redirect chain with a maximum depth, a cycle prevention rule and a test that proves a cycle cannot be created
The record specifies how an equated monthly instalment is categorised, separating principal from interest so principal movement is not reported as spending
The record is merged as ADR-016 in its own file, and the generated index and pending table in adr/README.md are refreshed by the T-ADR-INDEX-10 generator rather than hand-edited

items.title: ADR: ledger currency, foreign exchange reservation and debt balance derivation
items.outcome: One record fixes single-currency transactions for the minimum viable product, reserves the foreign exchange structures without building them, and settles that debt balances derive from liability accounts rather than being stored independently.
items.context: The zero-sum minor-unit constraint conflicts with cross-currency transactions, and debt current balance conflicts with ledger-derived balances. Both conflicts block the debt engine and the multi-currency work, and both need one consistent answer.
scope: One currency per ledger transaction for the minimum viable product, with the constraint expressed per currency
Reserved per-currency clearing accounts and linked exchange groups, defined but not implemented
Quoted rate, rate source and explicit fee fields reserved for the eventual implementation
Debt balances derived from liability account entries; lender statements recorded as timestamped reconciliation snapshots
Corrections expressed as explicit ledger adjustments rather than in-place edits
Published as the reserved record ADR-017 in its own file under adr/, claimed from the T-ADR-INDEX-10 reservation file
acceptance_criteria: The record states the zero-sum constraint precisely enough to be written as a database constraint
The record shows how a cross-currency exchange will be represented later without changing any existing stored amount
The record states that no stored debt balance is authoritative and specifies how a lender statement discrepancy is recorded
The record specifies whether a correction ever mutates a prior entry and rejects the alternative with a reason
The consequences for the debt engine, the split constraint and the multi-currency epic are named
The record reserves per-currency clearing accounts and states that a cross-currency movement is a group of single-currency entries that each balance within their own currency
The record requires a quoted rate, a rate source and a rate instant stored on the exchange, and forbids recomputing a historical figure from a later rate
The record requires every fee to be an explicit entry rather than being absorbed into the rate
The record specifies the exchange group as atomic: the whole group commits or none of it does, enforced in the database rather than in application code
The record specifies reversal as a paired reversal of the whole group, never a partial reversal of one leg
The record forbids any scalar total that mixes currencies and requires a per-currency breakdown with a stated derivation instead
The record states that multi-currency implementation remains in the moat phase and that only the reservations land earlier
The record is merged as ADR-017 in its own file, and the generated index and pending table in adr/README.md are refreshed by the T-ADR-INDEX-10 generator rather than hand-edited

items.title: ADR: encryption scope, searchable fields and row-level security
items.outcome: One record decides which columns are encrypted, which remain constrained and searchable, and how encrypted descriptive data is still searched, so the ledger invariants and the encryption requirement stop contradicting each other.
items.context: The security architecture requires transaction amounts to be stored as ciphertext while the ledger requires the database to sum and constrain them. Randomised ciphertext cannot be summed. Merchant text needs encryption but also normalisation, search and deduplication. Nothing currently resolves either conflict.
scope: Numeric constrained fields remain integer columns protected by row-level security and storage encryption
Descriptive personal data encrypted at the application layer with per-user data encryption keys
A normalised merchant dictionary or per-tenant blind index for the queries that must remain possible
Row-level security posture including forced policies, a low-privilege role and write checks
Explicit statement of what each choice leaks and what it does not protect against
Interaction with connection pooling and the session variable that carries tenant identity
Data, wrapping and blind-index key lifecycle covering generation, cadence, overlap, resumable rotation, retirement, emergency rotation and backup handling
Published as the reserved record ADR-018 in its own file under adr/, claimed from the T-ADR-INDEX-10 reservation file

Grant-mediated cross-user read design under forced row-level security: the exact policy predicate, the session context that carries the reader identity and the grant set, and the trusted setter that populates it

Deduplication artefacts across the device and server: a device-local raw-message digest, the server transaction dedupe key and the fuzzy duplicate-candidate match, with distinct names, construction and retention
acceptance_criteria: The record lists every candidate column and classifies it as constrained, encrypted or blind-indexed, with a reason
The record states that amounts are not application-layer encrypted and names the compensating controls
The searchable design states which query shapes remain possible and which are deliberately lost
Key separation between the data key and any index key is specified
Frequency-analysis leakage of the blind index is acknowledged with its mitigation
The record names the migration path and states that no ledger constraint is weakened
The record specifies rotation cadence and cryptoperiod for each key class and how old and new keys overlap without an availability gap
The record defines resumable re-encryption, retirement proof, emergency rotation and restore behavior without resurrecting retired key material
The record is merged as ADR-018 in its own file, and the generated index and pending table in adr/README.md are refreshed by the T-ADR-INDEX-10 generator rather than hand-edited
The record states the exact row-level security predicate that admits a grant-mediated cross-user read, naming the policy identifier, the tables it covers and the columns it compares

The record names the session context keys that carry the reading principal and the resolved grant set, and states that only a trusted setter function may write them, that the client role may not, and that they are cleared before a pooled connection is returned

The record forbids every bypass alternative by name - no BYPASSRLS role, no SECURITY DEFINER read that skips the predicate, no superuser connection and no disabling of FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY - and states that a cross-user read with no satisfied grant predicate is a denial rather than an empty-result convenience
The record states how the grant set is resolved and how long it may be cached inside one request, and that revocation invalidates it within the published bound

The record states that any digest derived from raw message text is keyed by a per-install key held in Android Keystore, remains only in the device-local raw-event store and is structurally absent from every API, sync and export schema

The record defines transactions.dedupe_key as a server-computed keyed fingerprint over canonical structured fields, not raw text, names its key class and rotation behaviour, and states what a database dump plus the shipped parser templates can and cannot recover

The record reconciles the exact local digest, the server structured fingerprint and the fuzzy amount-account-time-merchant candidate match; a fuzzy merge creates a reversible link and audit record rather than deleting either legitimate charge
The record explicitly supersedes only ADR-004's ambiguous raw-message-hash storage sentence while preserving the accepted decision that raw message content never leaves the device
contracts_schema: The decision record is itself the contract input; it names the schema, wire or interface consequences it forces
Publishes the stable identifier of the grant-mediating policy so the sharing contract and the sharing implementation both bind to the same database object rather than to prose
security_privacy: Names the security and privacy consequences of the chosen option and of the rejected options
Key rotation failure denies unsafe retirement, raises an alert and never leaves ciphertext without a usable authorized key
A cross-user read is admitted by a database policy predicate over an explicit grant, never by elevating the connection out of row-level security
observability: Names the signals that will prove the decision is being honoured in production
Names rotation age, progress, failure, stale-key and emergency-rotation signals
tests: Names the tests that implementation tickets must add to prove conformance
Names interrupted-and-resumed rotation, old-key retirement, emergency rotation and backup-restore tests
Names the negative test that a cross-user read with no satisfied grant predicate is denied, and the test that a forged or client-set session context cannot satisfy it
Names the contract test proving a raw-derived digest cannot be serialized, the preimage-resistance test for the server fingerprint and the false-merge unmerge test for two genuine identical charges

items.title: ADR: authentication, passkeys, provider, relying-party identifier and recovery
items.outcome: One record settles whether passkeys are in the minimum viable product, which provider is used, what the relying-party identifier is, how recovery works and whether sessions are device-bound, before any authentication code becomes Ready.
items.context: The security checklist requires passkeys for the minimum viable product while the identity epic defers them. Provider selection, relying-party identifier, recovery and device binding are all undecided, and a wrong relying-party identifier is effectively unfixable once credentials exist in the field.
scope: Passkey timing decision with a stated rationale rather than a silent deferral
Provider decision between a self-hosted identity server and a managed regional service, including the cost and exit considerations
Relying-party identifier and origin set across the Android application and the web application
Recovery paths and their abuse resistance, including what happens when every credential is lost
Session and refresh token model, rotation, reuse detection and whether tokens are device-bound
Phone verification and its relationship to trial abuse controls
Relying-party identifier and its Android Digital Asset Links companion published at the exact origin, with the rollout order stated
Related Origin Requests decision for every web origin that must share passkeys, including the current five-associated-origin limit and the fallback when the inventory exceeds it
Credential custody and portability: who holds the credential, whether it syncs with a platform password manager and how a user leaves
Lost-device recovery, single-use recovery codes, their storage and their regeneration
Cooling-off period on recovery and on credential change, and its interaction with device binding
Workload identity and non-forgeable delegated user context for api-to-ai-service and admin-to-api calls, separate from end-user bearer tokens
Published as the reserved record ADR-019 in its own file under adr/, claimed from the T-ADR-INDEX-10 reservation file
acceptance_criteria: The record names the chosen option for each of the six scope items and the options rejected
The relying-party identifier is stated exactly and the consequence of changing it later is quantified
The recovery design states its abuse resistance and what an attacker who controls the recovery channel can achieve
The record states whether refresh tokens are device-bound and how a legitimate device change is handled
The record lists the authentication tickets it unblocks and any that must be rewritten
The record states the exact relying-party identifier string and the full origin set, and quantifies the cost of changing it after credentials exist in the field
The record specifies the Android Digital Asset Links file, the signing certificate fingerprints it must carry and how a signing key rotation is handled without invalidating credentials

The record lists every related origin, verifies the well-known related-origins response, stays within the platform limit and states whether additional brands consolidate under one RP ID or require separate credentials
The record states credential custody and portability: whether credentials sync through a platform password manager, what happens on platform migration and what the user can export
The record specifies lost-device recovery end to end, including single-use recovery codes, how they are generated, displayed once, stored hashed and regenerated
The record specifies a cooling-off period for recovery and for credential changes, states its duration and states which capabilities are restricted during it
The record states whether sessions and refresh tokens are device-bound, and how a legitimate device change is distinguished from a takeover attempt

The record selects no identity vendor by name until the relying-party identifier, custody, recovery and device-binding requirements are settled, and records the evaluation criteria a later vendor decision must meet
The record selects the internal service authentication mechanism and states token or certificate audience, expiry, rotation and revocation semantics
The record defines how delegated user context is bound to an authenticated workload and rejects omitted, expired, replayed or caller-forged subject context

items.title: ADR: administrative boundary, deployment, database role and audit stream
items.outcome: One record fixes that the administrative interface is a separately deployed process on a distinct host with its own database role, policy boundary and audit stream, and that it never casually bypasses tenant isolation.
items.context: Administrative controls are described inconsistently across sources, some as minimum viable product and some as later work. Without a boundary decision the administrative surface will be built inside the customer application, which makes every staff account a total-compromise vector.
scope: Separate deployable process and host for the administrative interface
Distinct database role with its own grants and no reuse of the customer application role
Policy evaluation point that every administrative route passes through, default deny
Separate audit stream with write-once retention that administrators cannot delete from
Rule for when, if ever, an administrative path may read across tenants and what it must record
Separation of the administrative identity domain from customer identity
Published as the reserved record ADR-020 in its own file under adr/, claimed from the T-ADR-INDEX-10 reservation file
Explicit relationship between the three audit streams: the foundational application audit trail, the chained tamper-evident administrative audit log, and the subject-visible transparency stream
Store topology and write semantics for those three streams: which share a store, which are physically separate, and where a single write is projected versus dual-written
acceptance_criteria: The record states the deployment topology and rejects the in-application alternative with a reason
The record states the database grants for the administrative role and forbids direct production database access from the console
The record specifies that unredacted values are produced only by an approved unmask path, never by default
The record specifies that administrators never receive raw data encryption keys and names how that is enforced
The record states which controls are release blocking and which may follow, resolving the current inconsistency
The record is merged as ADR-020 in its own file, and the generated index and pending table in adr/README.md are refreshed by the T-ADR-INDEX-10 generator rather than hand-edited
The record names all three audit streams, states the purpose and the reader of each, and states which events appear in more than one
The record states, per stream, whether it has its own store or shares one, and whether an administrative action is a single write projected into the other streams or a dual write
Where a dual write is chosen, the record states what happens when the second write fails: whether the action is refused, compensated or reconciled, and which stream is authoritative

The record states that the subject-visible transparency stream never exposes administrative identity or internal reason codes beyond the published vocabulary, and that the chained administrative log is never reader-filtered into it by accident

items.title: ADR: shared-data erasure and cross-user key access
items.outcome: One record settles what happens to counterparty data when a user is erased, and how a grantee decrypts data belonging to another user, so that family and split features do not silently corrupt other people's balances.
items.context: Per-user data encryption keys have no cross-user read path, yet family sharing and split groups both require one. Separately, destroying a user's key would corrupt balances held by other members. Retention obligations for the two cases are also inconsistent.
scope: Cross-user read design: shared group key, re-encryption or a proxy decryption path, chosen with a reason
Revocation semantics so that removing a grant actually removes the ability to decrypt
Erasure semantics for records with more than one data subject
What survives erasure for a counterparty, in what form, and with what identifiers removed
Retention position reconciled against the actual applicable obligations rather than an inherited assumption

items.title: ADR: AI egress, runtime platform and Mode C custom endpoints
items.outcome: One record settles that all AI traffic routes through the backend, how egress restriction is implemented on the actual runtime rather than an assumed one, and whether a client-direct custom endpoint mode may exist at all.
items.context: The AI research assumes a network policy primitive from a container orchestrator that is not the chosen runtime, and it also offers a client-direct mode that would defeat server-side quota, audit and request forgery controls. Both must be settled before any AI implementation ticket starts.
scope: All AI traffic routed through the backend, with the client never holding a provider endpoint
Egress restriction implemented with the primitives available on the chosen runtime
Denied destination classes including private ranges, loopback, link-local and instance metadata
Custom endpoint registration model: register once, validate, pin the resolved address, audit
Client-direct custom endpoint mode explicitly rejected because it bypasses quota, audit, safety, revocation and request-forgery controls
Where the kill switch lives and who can operate it
Redirect handling, address pinning and normalisation rules applied before any egress comparison
Published as the reserved record ADR-022 in its own file under adr/, claimed from the T-ADR-INDEX-10 reservation file
acceptance_criteria: The record names the runtime and the exact mechanism used to deny private-range egress on it
The record forbids passing a base address in a request body and states the registration flow instead
The record prohibits client-direct provider traffic and requires every BYOK and custom-endpoint request to traverse the authenticated gateway
The record states that quota, audit and request forgery controls are server-side and cannot be satisfied by a client-side mode
The record names the adversarial tests that must pass before any custom endpoint is exposed
The record requires egress policy to be re-evaluated on every redirect hop, with the redirect target validated against the same deny list as the original destination
The record requires the resolved address to be pinned for the life of the request so a DNS rebinding between validation and connection cannot reach a private destination
The record denies IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses and any alternate textual encoding of a denied address, and names the normalisation applied before comparison
The record denies the container credential endpoint at 169.254.170.2 and the instance metadata service explicitly, in addition to the private, loopback and link-local ranges
The record states that arbitrary custom destinations remain disabled until the destination is registered, approved and pinned, and until every egress gate passes

items.title: ADR: entitlement and quota model, plan identity and usage accounting
items.outcome: One record fixes plan and feature identity, the dimensions quota is counted in, the model allowlist, how BYOK usage is treated, whether usage is event-sourced or a materialized counter, and the reset boundary, and it explicitly supersedes the conflicting entitlement sketches in the domain model and the stack document.
items.context: Two research documents describe entitlements differently. architecture/01-domain-model.md section 5 sketches one entitlement shape and architecture/03-stack-and-monetization.md section 8 sketches another, and they disagree about what a quota counts, what a plan identifies and where usage lives. Billing, the AI gateway and the quota contract all read those sketches, so the disagreement propagates into three repositories before anyone notices. The revenue argument for the product depends on server-side entitlement enforcement, which cannot be enforced against two schemas.
scope: Plan and feature identity: whether a plan is a version, a code or a row, and what identifies a feature independently of the plan that grants it
Quota dimensions: requests and tokens counted separately, with the unit, the rounding rule and the point of measurement stated for each
Model allowlist per plan, and the behaviour when a request names a model the plan does not list
BYOK treatment: which dimensions are counted, which are exempt, and what is still enforced when the user supplies the key
Usage accounting: event-sourced ledger versus materialized counter, with the reconciliation and replay consequences of the choice
Reset boundary: calendar or rolling, the time zone it is evaluated in, and what happens to an in-flight reservation across the boundary
Which of the two existing entitlement sketches is superseded, named by document and section
Published as the reserved record ADR-023 in its own file under adr/, claimed from the T-ADR-INDEX-10 reservation file
acceptance_criteria: The record states one plan and feature identity model and states which of the two existing sketches it supersedes, naming architecture/01-domain-model.md section 5 and architecture/03-stack-and-monetization.md section 8 explicitly

The record defines request quota and token quota as separate dimensions, each with its unit, its rounding rule and the point at which it is measured, and states that one cannot be inferred from the other
The record defines the per-plan model allowlist and states that a request naming an unlisted model is refused with a distinguishable result rather than silently downgraded to another model
The record states exactly which quota dimensions a BYOK request consumes and which it does not, and names the controls that still apply under BYOK
The record chooses event-sourced usage or a materialized counter, states the reason, and states how the other view is derived and reconciled
The record fixes the reset boundary and its time zone, and states what happens to a reservation that is open when the boundary passes
The superseded sketches are marked as superseded in place, so a reader who arrives at the old section is redirected rather than misled
The record states what an entitlement check returns when no plan resolves, and that the answer is a deny rather than a default plan
The record is merged as ADR-023 in its own file, and the generated index and pending table in adr/README.md are refreshed by the T-ADR-INDEX-10 generator rather than hand-edited
